

# Statistics and Plots from TrialLogger and EventLogger

##

`TrialLogger` and `EventLogger` both have a range of built-in useful helper functions and plots.



::: {.value-box fragment="fade-in" icon="fa-solid fa-lightbulb" icon-position="left" align="center" color="bg-green" value="Why use these rather than making my own plots?"}
There's nothing to stop you still making your own plots - and I'd actively encourage it!

But vidigi's plots have the benefit of being part of a tested ecosystem.

They will also hopefully save you time!
:::

## TrialLogger - Average durations

With `.get_event_duration_stat()`, we can easily pull out average durations for across the whole trial.

[TODO: Add in a by-run tweak to vidigi itself]

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| label: trial-logger-event-duration_stat_mean
my_trial.trial_logger.get_event_duration_stat(
    first_event="nurse_wait_begins",
    second_event="being_seen_by_nurse",
    what="mean",
    exclude_incomplete=True
    )
```


```{python}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| label: trial-logger-event-duration_stat_median
my_trial.trial_logger.get_event_duration_stat(
    first_event="arrival",
    second_event="depart",
    what="median",
    exclude_incomplete=True
    )
```


## TrialLogger - Duration Barplot

::: {style='font-size: 75%;'}
We can also look at this as a plot for multiple events at once.
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width='30%'}
First, we define our 'pairs' of events and give them some nicer names.
:::

::: {.column width='70%'}
```{python}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| label: trial-logger-event-pairs
event_pairs = [
        {"first_event": "nurse_wait_begins",
         "second_event":"being_seen_by_nurse",
         "label": "Nurse Wait Length"},
         {"first_event": "being_seen_by_nurse",
         "second_event":"nurse_treatment_ends",
         "label": "Nurse Treatment Length"},
         {"first_event": "arrival",
         "second_event":"depart",
         "label": "Full Journey Duration"},
]
```
:::

::::

Note that we're finally getting a chance to use that "nurse_treatment_ends" activity!

While it's still identically timed to *depart* here

- it is more intuitive to make use of it
- it avoids issues if we add more steps to our process down the line

## TrialLogger - Duration Barplot - Output



```{python}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| label: trial-logger-event-duration-barplot
my_trial.trial_logger.plot_metric_bar(
    event_pairs, what="mean",
    title= "Mean step durations",
    width=1000, height=400
    )
```

## TrialLogger - Queue length

`.plot_queue_size` allows us to see how queues changed across the course of our model run, for every run.

The black line indicates the average queue size, while the coloured lines show how the queue varied across runs.

[TODO: add CI to this plot in vidigi?]

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| label: trial-logger-queue-length
my_trial.trial_logger.plot_queue_size(
    ["nurse_wait_begins"],
    limit_duration=my_params.sim_duration,
    every_x_time_units=30, title="Nurse Queue Length",
    width=1000, height=450)
```


## Modifying these plots

Vidigi uses 'Plotly' throughout for its plots - which you've already had some experience with.

The Plotly objects it returns can be further modified if there is something you don't like about them or if they don't provide all of the options you need.

To do this, we first need to assign the plot to a variable so we can keep accessing it.

```{.python code-line-style="focus:1,dim:2-6" code-line-style-preset="emphasis"}
fig = my_trial.trial_logger.plot_queue_size(
    ["nurse_wait_begins"],
    limit_duration=my_params.sim_duration,
    every_x_time_units=30, title="Nurse Queue Length",
    width=1000, height=400
    )
```


## Modifying these plots (continued)

::::: {style='font-size: 80%;'}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width='30%'}
We can update something that already exists like the axis labels

:::

::: {.column width='70%'}
```{.python}
fig = my_trial.trial_logger.plot_queue_size(...)

fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Simulation time (minutes)")
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="People waiting")
```
:::

::::


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width='30%'}
Or adjust the layout - here we are reducing the margins

:::

::: {.column width='70%'}
```{.python}
fig.update_layout(margin=dict(l=20,r=20,t=40,b=20))
```

:::

::::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width='30%'}
Or add something completely new, like a horizontal reference line

:::

::: {.column width='70%'}
```{.python}
fig.add_hline(
    y=10, line_dash="dash",
    annotation_position="top left",
    annotation_text="Target max queue length"
    )
```
:::

::::

:::::


## Modifying these plots - output

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width='50%'}
We will need to use `.show()` to make the plot display.
:::

::: {.column width='50%'}
```{.python}
fig.show()
```
:::

::::


```{python}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| label: trial-logger-queue-length-edited
fig = my_trial.trial_logger.plot_queue_size(
    ["nurse_wait_begins"], limit_duration=my_params.sim_duration,
    every_x_time_units=30, title="Nurse Queue Length",
    width=1000, height=550)

# Change the axis labels
fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Simulation time (minutes)")
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="People waiting")

# Add a horizontal reference line
fig.add_hline(
    y=10, line_dash="dash",
    annotation_text="Target max queue length",
    annotation_position="top left"
)

fig.update_layout(
margin=dict(
        l=20,   # left
        r=20,   # right
        t=40,   # top
        b=20    # bottom
    )
)

HTML(fig.to_html(full_html=False, include_plotlyjs="cdn"))
```
